What does the chapter say about Iroquois neutrality before 1750?
column2: Not in the Ch. 6 text; the book only notes that the Iroquois claimed the Ohio Country by conquest and that Tanaghrisson wanted the French and British fighting each other to serve Iroquois interests.

column1: Why did Britain and France both want the Ohio Country?
column2: Britain wanted it for traders, land speculators, farmland and coal, while France wanted it as a buffer protecting Quebec.

column1: What happened on Washington's 1754 mission to the forks of the Ohio?
column2: The French had already built Fort Duquesne, Washington's men ambushed Jumonville's party, and a French force then made Washington surrender Fort Necessity.

column1: What was the significance of Washington's mission?
column2: It was the first step toward a long global war and set the pattern of early British defeats.

column1: What was the significance of Braddock's Defeat?
column2: It shocked the empire, emboldened the French, convinced wavering Indians to back France, and opened the backcountry to raids.

column1: Why did many Indians first ally with the French?
column2: The French generally took Indians more seriously than the English, while Braddock dismissed Indian land claims.

column1: Why did France's Indian alliances weaken?
column2: French officers denied warriors customary captives and plunder, and the 1757 British blockade cut off French trade goods and ammunition.

column1: What was the significance of capturing Louisbourg?
column2: It gave Britain control of the St. Lawrence River in 1758.

column1: What was the significance of capturing Quebec?
column2: Wolfe's 1759 victory led to Montreal's surrender in 1760, ending the war in North America.

column1: What did the Treaty of Paris give Britain?
column2: Britain got all French territory east of the Mississippi, Florida from Spain, Caribbean islands and Senegal.

column1: What did France and Spain lose or gain in 1763?
column2: France left North America, while Spain gave Florida to Britain but got back Cuba and took Louisiana west of the Mississippi.

column1: How did the British victory upset the balance of power?
column2: It removed France, so Indians lost a rival to play against Britain and colonists no longer needed British protection.

column1: What was the purpose of the Proclamation of 1763?
column2: It stopped settlement west of the Appalachians to ease Indian fears and prevent future wars.

column1: Why was the Proclamation of 1763 controversial with colonists?
column2: Colonists saw it as a betrayal, asking why they had fought France if the land won was set aside for Indians.

column1: What led to Pontiac's Rebellion?
column2: Indian war losses, Amherst's end to presents, higher prices from British traders and a flood of settlers led to it.

column1: What was the outcome of Pontiac's Rebellion?
column2: Bouquet stopped the offensive at Bushy Run, Amherst was recalled, and Britain changed its policy with the Proclamation of 1763.

column1: How did Britain use its victory to justify taxing the colonies?
column2: Britain argued that it fought the costly war to secure the colonies and needed troops to hold the gains, so the colonists who benefited should pay.

column1: How did Parliament view representation?
column2: Parliament held to virtual representation, in which each member represents the whole empire.

column1: How did colonists view representation?
column2: Colonists held to actual representation, in which only officials they elected could tax them.

column1: What was the Stamp Act?
column2: It was a 1765 direct tax for revenue on documents, newspapers, diplomas, cards and dice, with violators tried without juries.

column1: Why did the Stamp Act generate opposition?
column2: It taxed colonists without their consent, denied jury trials, and hit everyone during a postwar recession.

column1: How did upper-class colonists oppose the Stamp Act?
column2: Colonial leaders passed resolves in the assemblies and wrote pamphlets warning of a conspiracy against liberty.

column1: How did common colonists oppose the Stamp Act?
column2: Sailors, dockworkers, artisans and servants joined Sons of Liberty crowds that burned stamp distributors in effigy and wrecked their offices and homes.

column1: How did merchants oppose the Stamp Act?
column2: Merchants in Boston, New York and Philadelphia boycotted English goods to make British traders lobby for repeal.

column1: What finally led to repeal of the Stamp Act?
column2: Rockingham replaced Grenville, and London merchants hurt by nonimportation backed repeal in March 1766.

column1: Why did Parliament pass the Townshend Acts?
column2: Parliament wanted to raise revenue and curb colonial assemblies by paying royal officials from the new duties.

column1: Why did so many colonists react strongly against the Townshend Acts?
column2: Colonists saw them as more taxation without consent and more proof that they were not treated like the English.

column1: How successful were the boycotts?
column2: Nonimportation helped win Stamp Act repeal and led Parliament to repeal all Townshend duties except tea in 1770.

column1: What was the reality of the Boston Massacre?
column2: A heckled squad of soldiers fired into a snowball-throwing crowd, and Preston and four soldiers were acquitted, with two convicted of manslaughter.

column1: What was the propaganda version of the Boston Massacre?
column2: Samuel Adams and the Boston Gazette portrayed it as a deliberate atrocity, printing a black-bordered issue with five coffins.

column1: What did the Sons of Liberty do to resist British policy?
column2: They organized crowds that forced stamp distributors to resign and targeted customs collectors.

column1: What role did the committees of correspondence play?
column2: They spread statements of grievances within and among the colonies, building an intercolonial network that carried resistance into rural areas.

column1: Why did Bostonians hold the Tea Party?
column2: They refused to accept Parliament's taxing power through cheap tea and the demand to send the tea back to England was refused.

column1: What happened at the Boston Tea Party?
column2: About 50 men disguised as Indians dumped 90,000 pounds of tea from three ships at Griffin's Wharf.

column1: Why did the Coercive Acts spark outrage?
column2: They punished all of Massachusetts and ended its self-government, which colonists saw as proof of a plot to enslave them.

column1: What were the goals of the First Continental Congress?
column2: It aimed to define American rights, set the limits of Parliament's power, and choose tactics against the Coercive Acts.

column1: What happened at Lexington?
column2: About 70 minutemen faced 700 British troops on Lexington Green, an unknown shot set off volleys, and 8 Americans died.

column1: What happened at Concord?
column2: Militia at the North Bridge fired with deadly accuracy, and the British retreated to Boston under fire.

column1: What happened after Lexington and Concord?
column2: About 20,000 New England militia besieged Boston.
